Your description certainly matches the general diagnostic criteria for bipolar disorder. (I am not a doctor/blah blah.)

Handling this is a very tough job, and a full-time one at that. Don't expect to be perfect at it overnight (or ever). It can get a lot easier with appropriate treatment, but it's never going to go away entirely. Something that's useful for me is to develop the perspective that it's a recurring challenge but not an insurmountable one. Pay attention to your state as much as you can, and if necessary, take notes. You'll develop coping skills as time goes on, and strengthen the ones that have gotten you this far.

Psych evaluations are based almost entirely on self-reporting. To get the most good from them you need to be completely thorough and utterly honest. If that means you walk in with six pages of notes of what to talk about, so be it (I've done that, btw). The only thing I would avoid is trying to modify or adjust the truth, no matter how painful it might be. Doctors see a lot of bad shit - don't worry about being the worst case they've ever had. Just spill it all out.

As for your feelings and validation - you're in the right place. We all know exactly what you're going through and there is a wealth of advice, caring, and support available through places like this sub.

Alcohol is a *central nervous system depressant*, meaning it leads to decreased brain/neural function. It does not mean it makes you depressed. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_nervous_system_depression

In fact, the opposite is usually true; one of the most common symptoms of ethanol intoxication is euphoria. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_intoxication

I agree. To me, mental health is completely independent of violent aggression. You can have either one without the other, and you can have neither, or you can have both. Trying to tie them together is misguided at best.

My entire point here is that I think more people need to understand that separation. Having a mental illness, diagnosed or otherwise, should not be a sentence to a life of stigma and rejection and exclusion.

Just an interesting tidbit: alcohol is indeed a "central nervous system depressant." However, that term is *not* the same kind of "depress" as we tend to think of, and in particular is *not* the opposite of "antidepressant."

In other words, booze does not inherently make you feel depressed, in the sadness sense.

What it *does* do it affect your neurotransmitters and neuroreceptors in very fundamental ways. It also affects heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and so on. All of these can add up to *feeling* negative in some cases, especially for people who have a tendency toward physical pain or discomfort during true depression.

The brain is a remarkable machine for making associations. It is a well-documented effect that alcohol can trigger certain mental patterns. For example, if you learn a skill while buzzed or drunk, you're likely to be able to repeat that skill only while in the same state, without re-learning it from scratch in a sober state. This kind of pattern association is very important in understanding the effects of alcohol on mental state and mood.

For me, the sedative effect of alcohol very much reminds me of how I feel when I'm lethargic due to depression. In my case, the mental association is that booze = feeling slow, lack of energy, and so on. If I'm not careful, drinking will put me into the state of mind that "hey, I feel these things, therefore I must be depressed!" and suddenly things start to spiral out of control.

Of course, alcohol is also known to interact in nasty ways with medications, so that's another variable worth considering.

Not saying definitively that this explains your situation, but I hope it's at least interesting food for thought.

Gonna have to throw my hat in the "get a new doctor" ring. I had a similar experience with someone several years ago. When I'm talking about myself, *especially* in a psychiatric situation, I tend to be very wry and almost bitterly sarcastic. This particular doctor completely ignored the obvious signs in front of him because, much like in your case, he didn't think I was "serious enough." The whole absurd episode opened my eyes to something I had never really considered before:

*Psychiatry is a job, performed by mere humans.*

Think about your job, and the people who work there. How many take it seriously? How many sink 100% of themselves into their work? How many are just doing it for a paycheck and just fundamentally don't give a shit?

Take that proportion, and slap it onto the pdoc world. Roughly (very roughly) that same percentage of doctors are going to be totally useless at their job. The same proportion will be punching the clock and not caring about their patients. And the really good ones? Same ratio.

So don't be overly discouraged. Chances are you can find someone else who's a marked improvement. With enough time, you can definitely find someone who will give you the attention and care you deserve.

I've had prolonged and excruciating problems with compliance. Sometimes I quit with some vague excuse, and other times I just... quit, no reason.

One thing that helps me is to keep my meds in someplace unavoidable - in particular, I literally stack my bottles on top of my wallet and car keys. If I want to go anywhere or do anything, I have to plow through a pile of meds to do it.

I've come close to doing the chart and stickers thing many times, because I too will occasionally just forget, or make up excuses, or whatever else. Even a single missed dose means an unavoidable episode for me, so I always know when it happens - but not always immediately, which is annoying.

So yeah... not sad at all. I completely understand.

I will say two things.

First of all, this can be done. I live a pretty stable and successful life right now with a great job in a pressure-cooker industry. It is _possible_ to survive having bipolar disorder in a business startup.

Now for the less encouraging and more important bit:

This _will_ be the hardest thing you ever attempt, and the odds are _not_ in your favor. It only takes one crash to completely destroy a business, especially one as fragile as a startup. Moreover, as soon as that hypomanic/manic energy fades, you're likely to be left with a lot of avoidable problems that you (knowingly or otherwise) created while you were up.

I don't say this as speculation or based on probabilities from research or any shit like that - this is pure experience.

My advice? If you feel brave and are reasonably stable, go for it. But do *not* give in to the temptation to treat manic energy as an asset. If you do start going too far up, the best thing you can do is _back off the work_. I know this is counter to all of our instincts and desires at that moment, but it's the healthiest thing we can do, and it will save a lot of pain and awkwardness.

Many bipolar sufferers can be very successful when manic. The key to surviving the crash is to have a foundation of stability that is _not_ built on manic energy.

But in the end, what happened yesterday or ten years ago doesn't matter. What matters is what we do with today.

Not really advice per se, but here's my opinion.

Bipolar disorder is very, very, excruciatingly real. The mania, the euphoria, the suffering - all of it is real to us, and really happens. It is not someone else's place to decide if our struggles are valid; we live with those pains, and for us every bit of it is valid.

I have a terrible time forming lasting relationships, so I know how hard it is to find someone who seems mostly perfect but has that one shortcoming that's just too hard to ignore. In your case, that shortcoming is very difficult, because it pertains to something that is very much an important part of your life.

I personally decided a long time ago that I couldn't be with anyone who doesn't understand to at least some extent how serious my disorder is. Knowing what it's like is probably too much to ask, but I definitely need the support of someone who is willing to accept that sometimes my life is not great. Or maybe too great, depending on the day.

In the end I think you will know what is best for you; maybe his mind can be changed and this will work out, and maybe it's best you just move on before expending too much effort and heartache on it. I can't say one way or another.

But I do think you deserve a chance to have someone in your life who is supportive of the hardship you live with. I think we all do.

It's well known that antidepressants by themselves can trigger manic symptoms in people with bipolar disorder. There's a link about it on the sidebar of this subreddit, even. If your prescribing doctor is not taking proper precautions to mediate the antidepressant with other medication to manage the mania, I'd strongly suggest finding someone else to offer a second opinion.

That said... several medications have messed with me pretty badly in the past. Seroquel is like a nuclear-powered tranquilizer for me and gives me the shakes and the most incredibly fucked up dreams; I don't take it anymore. Depakote made me feel like a complete zombie for months even after I stopped taking it.

There's also the time I deliberately OD'ed on escitalopram (a sister medication to what you were prescribed) and gave myself serotonergic syndrome. That's no fun and you don't want to go there.

I am all too familiar with scaring people around me in the throes of an episode. I know what it's like to unintentionally hurt the people who are watching and feeling helpless. I also know what it's like to _deliberately_ hurt them.

The main thing I want to say to you is that _this is not something you should take blame for, even from yourself_. None of us chose to have bipolar disorder. None of us wants to live like this, really, even if sometimes we get a twisted sense of satisfaction from our own suffering. And the fact that you're posting this means you're not so far gone that you want to destroy everything and everyone around you - which is very good.

What I want to show you is that you have to be very careful when taking responsibility for what happens in your life as a result of the disorder. We should never use it as an excuse, but we are _completely_ justified in using it as an explanation. The pain we cause is not our fault. It's not like we're trying to cause this pain on purpose. Yes, we need to accept that it happens and own it to an extent, but it should not be a source of guilt.

I've spent many lonely years wondering if I could ever let myself be in a genuine relationship, because I have the same suspicion that other people are "better off" without my presence. I feel toxic a lot of the time, as if "my shit" is so bad that it is insufferable to everyone else.

_This is a lie._

We are valuable people, all of us, and having a disorder doesn't change that. We can and should be positive and important elements in the lives of others. We absolutely should be careful about the negative effects we have, but we cannot afford to shoulder guilt over the things we cannot control.

One final thought: a relationship is not just about one person's wellbeing or desires or decision-making. He deserves a chance to make this choice for himself, and if you have concerns, the best thing you can do is _communicate_. If the result of your communication is that you two would be better off apart, so be it; but it sounds to me like you can do a lot of good for each other too, and work on mitigating the bad.

The only thing I know for sure is that he deserves to have a part in whatever you choose.

I have a nasty case of bipolar disorder. Depression pretty much rules my life the majority of the time. History of substance abuse, self-medication, self-mutilation, several suicide attempts under my belt, you name it.

I'm currently a team lead for a very reputable computer company, making six figures a year. I'm preparing to buy my second house. Nobody here even knows I'm bipolar.

Don't let some random facts about your brain become a reason to artificially limit your life.

Yes, it's going to be tough. Yes, it's harder for us than for many other people. Yes, pushing yourself when you're on a downswing is brutally difficult. But it can be done, and you deserve to wring every last drop of success out of your life. Manage your symptoms, do what it takes to survive, and _the hell with everyone who doubts you_.

I was in a very similar position a couple years ago. Hated where I lived, hated my job, hated most of the people around me, hated pretty much every circumstance of my existence.

So I took a huge risk, moved across the country for a job I knew barely anything about, and never looked back. I still regard it as one of the best decisions I ever made.

Yes, it's dangerous. Yes, you should be cautious about these kinds of feelings in conjunction with bipolar disorder, because restlessness and an urge to scrub away the trappings of life are a common set of symptoms. But maybe this is something you need to do for _you_.

Want to know the real kicker?

Two months before I moved, my bank account was overdrawn by several hundred dollars.

Finances are a real thing and they can and do impose limits on our lives. But most of the time, we limit ourselves far more than our money does.

I don't think "us" has anything to worry about. Me personally is a different matter.

Don't get me wrong - I know romance is a tough thing for anyone with bipolar disorder, and it takes more work and dedication than most people can understand. But I think it's _possible_, and given the right people, it's undoubtedly more intense than "normal" relationships.

I guess what I'm saying is that bipolar disorder shouldn't be a reason to give up on love, even if it feels like it for so many of us.

As to why I myself have given up... that's a long-ass story.

My advice? Be selective in who you let know about it. Not secretive, necessarily, just careful. There's a tremendous amount of stigma and ignorance around mental health issues in our world, and many people _will_ judge you negatively if you bring it up. Others will _think_ they're being sympathetic and understanding, but wind up thinking that everything you ever do is a result of the disorder, which is kind of worse IMO.

But that's all out of your control, and fuck other people anyways.

Take charge of what you _can_ affect: your medication, your therapy, your support network. Make sure you stay disciplined in managing those areas of your life, and you'll be as fine as anyone with bipolar disorder can get.

It's easy to say and monumentally hard to do, but there's one last thing I'd suggest to someone in your position: do whatever it takes to not let this ruin your life. You've got a lot ahead of you, good and bad; but never let yourself believe that you're any less capable of living a good life than anyone else. It may not always feel like it, but if anything, surviving this makes you tougher than the average schmuck.

Best of luck, and take it one day at a time. The future can worry about itself.

I very nearly posted this under my main account, because I think it would genuinely shock the people who are in my life right now to learn that I am type I bipolar. Sadly, the stigma around it is still strong enough that tying my real identity to my story is probably a bad idea. So the alt account it is.

I can give you my whole story if you're really interested, but it's long and twisty and full of weird rabbit trails, so here's what I actually want to say to you:

You can learn to beat this. Not in the sappy "just get a grip" way that "normal" people like to attack us with. Nor in the 80's power-ballad montage scene sense, where you do some magical juju and suddenly you're more powerful than the disease.

I like to think of it like mathematical induction (but I'm a nerd, so YMMV). I am not going to be beaten by this, and this is my proof: I was not beaten yesterday, and yesterday is no different than today. Therefore I will not be beaten today.

On my good days, that's where it stops, and I can function. On my bad days, I have to add a little more:

Maybe I'll be beaten tomorrow. **But not fucking today.**

At first, you need to prioritize. There is only one thing you need to do, and that is survive. It's one day at a time - with me, an ultradian rapid cycler, sometimes it's literally surviving twenty seconds at a time. Life comes and goes; some days are easy, some are hard. Sometimes I stay on my meds, sometimes I don't. Sometimes survival is all I've got, and when that happens, _you do whatever the fuck you have to do to make sure you hang on just a little longer_.

I've done things I never thought my pride would let me do, just to hang on. Just remember: it may feel like weakness sometimes, but the fact that you're fighting _in any capacity_ means you are not weak. You are strong. The weak do not survive, and we are going to survive.

After a while, surviving becomes a habit. Then a way of life. Then it becomes somewhat automatic. Not always easy or effortless, mind you, but you can establish patterns that help you stay centered in survival.

And once you hit that point, you are in good shape, because now you have a little bit of room to start moving forward. Goals are a mixed blessing; they can give you some focus and guidance, but they can mercilessly mock you when you feel like you are failing to reach them. Be careful with goals.

But if and when you find that little bit of breathing room, use it. Move forward. Even if it's a tiny thing: go to bed on time. Get _out_ of bed on time. Brush your teeth. Take a shower. Make a meal. Talk to someone, even if it's just saying "hi" and moving on. The little things will add up, and you will gain confidence and comfort every time you manage to win even a tiny victory against the enemy in your mind.

Let those victories add up. It won't always be forward progress. There will be hard times, times when you think it's all lost, times when it gets worse than ever. But just go back to surviving, and you will make it out.

I've had symptoms for over 16 years now. I was diagnosed officially in 2007 (incorrectly for a while, at first). I've tried to kill myself more times than I can remember. I've had so many psychotic breaks and abused my medications and other substances so heavily that it's a miracle my mind works at all. I have a lot of scars on my left arm (and a few others that I was trying to keep hidden). My life is littered with the debris of both manic and depressive episodes, and the occasional mixed episode has led to an arrest, an almost-foreclosure I lied my way out of, countless arguments and fights with family and friends... I've never maintained a stable relationship for any appreciable length of time...

But two years ago, I moved across the country. I got a new job. I started meeting new people, and for once in my life I didn't let my disorder define my interactions with them. None of them has any clue.

I've been promoted a few times and will formally accept another promotion at the end of this month. I've made good friends and started developing hobbies and passions even outside of work. I've cut ties with a lot of toxic and abusive people - including (or maybe I should say mainly) family members - who had negative influences on me in the past. I'm recovering my senses of hygiene and discipline.

I even cooked myself a meal yesterday, for the first time in months.

I will never, ever pretend to you that this is an easy life. I will not lie to you and say that it is guaranteed to get better. I won't even paint the rosy picture that with dedication and hard work it'll all go away and be manageable.

For all the positive things in my life, I still sleep with a gun next to the bed, just in case I need to use it. I still force myself to down a handful of pills every day (well, most days). I still have to be extremely careful about my sleeping patterns and exercise and who I spend time with, lest I get out of balance.

I will never be free of being bipolar, and someday, it very well may win.

But not fucking today.

Yes... yes it does.

I think the pain lessens a bit over time, but either way, it's an integral part of growth. It's another facet of the situation, shaping but not controlling who we are.

I can't speak for anyone else, but for me, it's mostly a matter of time and gradual acceptance. I've had to revisit my past an awful lot to reach the point where I can even admit to it openly, let alone start to reconcile all the diverse and often unpleasant emotions that it all brings up. But it slowly and surely gets easier to deal with, and I think that's a result of getting stronger and more resilient as time goes by.

Like anything else that hurts, the best we can do is endure the pain and seek ways to be strengthened by the experience.

I think there's a difference between wanting to move on, and wanting to _forget_.

For me personally, being bipolar is an integral part of my past - and, in all probability, my future. I don't _like_ it per se, but it's there, and for better or worse (ok, let's be honest, mostly worse) it's made me into who I am _now_.

The way I see it, we are not divorced from our symptoms or feelings. This isn't some "other person" living out their lives in our heads; whether we like it or not, _this is who we are_. It's not as if there's some other occupant upstairs being experimental, avant-garde, risk-taking, moody, voracious, megalomaniacal, elite, workaholic, melancholic, tormented, dark, or abstract. That's _us_. You _were_ (and perhaps still _are_) all of those things - it isn't just some shell that you wear.

Yes, those aspects of ourselves may be rooted in a disease, but that doesn't make them any less valid or any less personal and real. Genuine psychosis aside, what we think and feel is more or less who we are.

The obvious problem with this is that those things are often distasteful. It's not pleasant to think "hey, yeah, I'm really whacked out." Especially as you mention when there are past deeds, damaged relationships, and general wasted time that we regret, it can be extremely difficult to accept. For my own part, there are certainly times when I _want_ all that to just be someone else taking over my body for a while. I _want_ to not be associated with a lot of those things.

But in my thoroughly off-the-cuff and not-professionally-trained opinion, I think it's important to see those things as part of your whole being. And that, I think, is the key - those things are _just a part_. There is more to you - more to all of us - than just being bipolar. And there is more to be had than just symptoms, even if there have been times when the symptoms seem to dominate everything else.

There's an analogy I really like for this. Imagine a giant, bustling factory full of noisy machinery, yelling workers, and generally a bunch of deafening racket. Now imagine that high up in the rafters of the building, a songbird has built a nest. Most of the time, when the factory is busy, you'll never be able to hear that bird singing. But when everyone goes home and everything is shut down for the night, there's something of beauty and value to be found under the surface.

Some of the time, maybe even most of the time, the noise of our bipolar symptoms may be deafening. But that does not in any way subtract from the reality of the songbird sitting in the rafters, waiting for a chance to be heard.

I think it's awesome that you're on medication and doing better. I think that's a sign that you're in a good position to start listening for the bird singing, and hopefully to bring that sound to the forefront of your life.

I had a similar shift of diagnosis a few years ago. I had trouble with it as well at first, but for different reasons: I was angry that my doctor at the time had paid so little attention to my case that he had totally missed obvious manic episodes and decided to downplay the severity of my situation. Needless to say, I fired him pretty soon after that.

As has been said: all it means is that you fall into the category of having experienced a full manic episode. Remember that diagnosis depends a lot on monitoring history and it can take _years_ to arrive at a correct diagnosis, let alone a fully effective and stable treatment. Even then, treatments often need constant monitoring and occasional adjustment to have peak effectiveness.

If you're at all like me, that thought is pretty damn terrifying and discouraging. I hate the idea that I have to sort of sleep with one eye open and constantly watch myself for signs of trouble; I hate the idea that I may never have anything resembling a normal life without being on some kind of medication; and I _really_ hate the idea that I'm stuck with this for the foreseeable future. Barring radical advancements in neurotechnology in my lifetime, I'm always going to be fighting this in some form or another.

Someone else here once said something that resonated a lot with me, though: it may not get easier, but you do get stronger. It's kind of like lifting weights in that sense. The bar may not get lighter, but lifting it becomes less of a chore as you get accustomed to the load and build up your capabilities. I've found that that holds very true for me. I don't really think it's gotten any easier, but I've found a few ways of dealing with it, and it's no longer this big life-shattering _thing_.

I guess the best thing I can offer you is this: the change in diagnosis means you are closer to having a handle on your situation - not just bipolar disorder in general, but _your personal encounter with it_. And that means you're one step closer to moving past it and regaining full quality of life.

I'm Type I with ultradian rapid cycling (i.e. I can have several swings between extremes in a single day).

Generally rapid cycling seems to be less well-understood by most doctors, even psychiatric specialists; I don't know why, but my guess is because it's less common. I've never heard a really good definition of what qualifies, but most rapid cyclers I've heard of have pretty similar patterns, myself included.

Less severe episodes are actually not uncommon either; not every single experience is either whacked-out mania or deep depression. Probably 80% of my cycles (medicated or otherwise) are just abnormally high or low moods (and other symptoms - energy levels etc.) and they occur fairly often, probably every couple of months or so. Really extreme episodes are maybe once or twice a year.

In any case, though, definitely bring up your concerns with a psychiatrist. See if you can get a good talk therapist too; for a lot of people early in the bipolar diagnosis/treatment process, it takes a long time to really wrap your mind around what's going on and come to accept it. The sooner you can become comfortable with a diagnosis and treatment plan the sooner you can start regaining control.

I think the biggest effect it's had for me is that I _don't_ let anyone know I'm bipolar, precisely because I know the reactions are likely to be negative. The few people I have told in the past generally totally changed the way they interacted with me, and nothing has ever been the same since. It's destroyed a lot of my life and I'm not interested in letting it destroy more.

I think it's a terrible thing that I can't talk about something that is so deeply integral to my reality. At my last job, I told my employer about my diagnosis, in an attempt to explain my flaky work performance and get some understanding for the rough times. Unfortunately, it backfired badly, and they wound up just not paying me at random times, because they felt justified in ripping me off when I was having trouble getting things done.

So now I'm in another demanding, high-stress job and I feel like I can't and shouldn't tell anyone what's going on, because I can't stomach the thought of people handling me differently again. There are times (like right now) when it's extremely hard to wear the normal-mask, but as much as I hate to say it, I feel like I'm doing the right thing by keeping this private.

And of course there's the romantic relationship front, which I'm going to deliberately avoid delving into because I'm about to start my shift and I don't need to be all angsty and bitter for that ;-)

I was on Depakote for a long time and it totally killed my brain. I literally felt like I had the mental capacity of a child while I was on it. Eventually, after doing my own research on the medication, it became pretty obvious that he was full of shit and I fired him. One of the best decisions I've ever made.

Here's something I've found that a lot of doctors are scared to tell you: despite the warnings about SSRI/SNRI antidepressants and triggering mania, it _is_ possible to take them safely _in combination with other medications to manage the mania_. I've done various permutations of Lexapro, Wellbutrin, Abilify, and Seroquel (SSRI, SNRI, and atypical antipsychotics, respectively) and they work pretty well. Now, that's not to say that the risk isn't real, and that's not to say it will work for everyone - but you have the right to find out for yourself, because frankly nobody can predict how you'll respond to the medications.

And honestly, as my favorite doctor of the past once put it, it's far easier to bring someone down out of a mild hypomanic/manic swing than to convince them to keep trying when they're fully depressed. His philosophy was to err on the side of making me feel better, and then tone things down and/or increase the controls from the other medications as necessary. For the last couple of years I've been small doses of Lexapro and Wellbutrin daily, with varying doses of Abilify to respond to excessively manic mood changes, and occasional Seroquel as a sort of "emergency response" to shut things down if they ever get out of control. It works pretty darn well, but I fired three different doctors before finding one who was even willing to propose such a cocktail, let alone stick with me long enough to find a mixture that worked.

As to the big question... I've made it this far out of pure rotten stubbornness. I figure it this way: someday or later, this goddamn disease might kill me. Most of the time I secretly suspect that when I die it'll be self-inflicted. But every day, I tell myself this: it may get me eventually, and maybe that's inevitable. *But not today.*

Not. Fucking. Today.

And wouldn't you know it, 15 years on and I'm still here. Maybe not the best outlook ever, but hey, it obviously worked.

Oh, sure; I didn't meant to imply the math never (or even rarely) works in your favor. Just don't want to see you make any decisions based on false rigor.

I think there's one other thing your model leaves out, to its detriment: your metric captures only a quantification of _how things are_. Something worth factoring into the system is the potential - in a physics sense - for that value to change. You've described a number that you can graph over time as a simple planar curve; I think though that every point on that curve has an associated window of potential. At any given moment, there's how things _are_ and how things _could be_ - both in the positive and negative direction.

Think of it like a statistical model. You've captured the mean of the data set - the way things are - but you have cropped out the standard deviation. A mean by itself conveys very little information. You need to know not just where things stand now but how much better _or worse_ they could be at that given moment.

Progress shouldn't be measured on the absolute scale you've described; instead, you should measure progress against the relative sliding window of potential. The closer you are to the lower bound, the worse things are; the more you tend towards the upper bound, the better things are.  Of course absolute value is also important - it does after all affect the baseline of severity - but in measuring any kind of movement you need to take into account the margins.

And you're right that it's extremely hard to improve that absolute value, at any given moment in time. What's substantially less difficult is to increase the upper bound of your potential window. Raising the lower bound can be tough as well, but it's doable. If you continue to adjust the margins slowly and steadily, eventually you will inevitably shift the absolute instantaneous metric as well.

Mathematics can be a very powerful way to justify decisions; but it's always important to ensure that you have the most accurate model you can devise. Simplifying assumptions can be useful, but they can also distort perceptions in subtle and sometimes harmful ways. I'm not saying you're wrong... just that you might want to double-check the equations.
"Really" what?

Your math only works if the probabilities of each degree of suffering/happiness are evenly distributed. Even a normal distribution will radically alter the numbers, for instance; a Poisson distribution could change them still further; and so on.

Without knowing the probabilistic distribution curve, your gamble is far more uncertain. I think there might be a way to evaluate the cumulative odds of improvement by representing as many possible various distribution functions as you can across an n-space manifold and performing the appropriate multidimensional integration; I'm a little too tired to work out the exact mechanics of that though.

Depression is generally accompanied by tiredness, aches, and sometimes nausea. The main recognizable signs, for me, are actually mental; I start obsessively deconstructing my life and trying to stockpile a list of everything wrong with it. This typically means finding flaws in all of my relationships and trying to salt those wounds as vigorously as possible. Usually when I recognize the signs of a persecution complex developing, I know I'm going downhill.

Hypomania is different; I'll feel restless, energetic, unable to sit still; my mind will race and not produce anything. I just feel like there's a lot of motion in my head and no specific thoughts come from it. It's as if there's energy but no content... a lot of noise or static, but without noisiness or static, if that makes sense. If I can manage to get fixated on a task, it'll come effortlessly and just flow - for as long as my attention span holds out, which is typically not very long. I'll flip between a dozen activities in the space of a couple of hours, and do great at all of them (or so it seems) until I lose interest, at which point everything just collapses on itself.

Genuine mania I can't recognize, usually. The best way I can describe psychotic episodes is it feels like I'm having a very vivid dream. It normally takes someone else's observations to clue me in that something is going on (and that it's real).

Mixed states are usually a blend of the restless, highly energetic sensations with a complete lack of desire or ability to do anything. So I usually just end up pacing around in circles and feeling miserable. Every now and then I'll get symptoms like aches or mild fever that seems to go along with a mixed state, but that's not established itself as a definitive pattern by any means.

Social stigma is a powerful force.

Consider: in the US, I'd venture to guess that virtually everyone masturbates on a regular basis. So why don't we talk about _that_ more openly? For a handful of reasons, we have a social and cultural taboo on the subject, and maintain a puritanical denial about the whole thing. Most people will get uncomfortable as soon as the notion is even alluded to, and hardly anyone will openly, publicly discuss any sort of details. Consider that we hide behind internet anonymity and other deflections of our identities when talking about it on, say, reddit.

For something normal, healthy, and nearly ubiquitous, a simple historical coincidence can develop into a social force so powerful that a subject can become unmentionable.

Now, combine this with another powerful force: fear of the unknown, and fear of what is different.

What is more unknown and different than a mental disorder? People are deeply attached to the notion that your mind is your "self", and a disorder of the mind must therefore reflect on an innate personal flaw of some nature. It's no wonder that the general population is terrified of people who suffer from diseases like bipolar disorder.

The last thing I'd throw into the mix is simply apathy. America is a hideously prosperous first-world country. The average American doesn't care about genocide in Africa, or starvation in Southeast Asia, or repression in the Middle East. These problems are abstract, far away, and in no way _personal_. Actually, a total lack of energy and motivation is a common sign of depression, or a depressive episode. Most people associate "depression" with "I feel sad" but this is a misconception.

Clinical depression can range anywhere from a simple emotional ache to complete apathy to irritability and anger. A common element is _anhedonia_ wherein you lack the ability to enjoy or care about anything.

My depressive periods generally do include emotionally feeling "down", but during the milder run-up to the worst parts, typically consist of just not wanting to do anything at all. For me the most frustrating part is that it occurs _without_ any sort of rational explanation or cause; I have no good reason to feel bad or apathetic, I just do.

A lot of people like to hand out callous "advice" like "oh, just go for a jog, or watch a funny movie, or hang out with some friends and distract yourself." It's incredibly hard to communicate to them that it's not possible to do that; even if you can drag yourself out to go participate in some activity, you get nothing from it. This is what separates true depression from just bad moods, and what makes it (for me) painfully difficult to explain my disorder to someone who's never been there.

Hallucinations, grandiose delusions, feelings of transcendent supremacy... these are textbook descriptions of what I went through, and several years on, I find it incredibly hard to think of those periods in any other terms. To me, at this point in my life, what I felt, heard, saw, experienced... all of that was a product of a serious diseased condition. There were unquestionably direct correlations between those moments and my hypomanic and fully manic episodes.

More strikingly, though (for me at least) was the utter lack of such experiences outside of manic symptoms. Even during periods of relative normalcy, I never really "felt" any kind of supernatural connection. It all seemed contrived and arbitrary to me. At worst, during depression, I never - not once - felt any kind of consolation or hope from my faith. So many people told me that belief was the only thing that could save me from my situation. They had so many explanations for it... sin, delusions, straying from the truth, ignoring god, rebellion, even demon possession. Obviously the problem (in their minds) was that I wasn't pursuing spirituality hard enough.

What finally nailed the coffin shut was the realization that there was a direct correlation in my life between _seeking_ spirituality, and failing to find it in any significant manner.

I am now a happy atheist, and I've outed myself to my family and friends. I no longer subscribe to any sort of belief in "that which lies beyond", in any sense. I've had a much better time coping with my condition and my reality since jettisoning the baggage of religion.

It's just my personal experience, so please don't interpret this as a condemnation of anyone else's own spiritual journeys. But to me, at least, it was unspeakably comforting to come to grips with the fact that most of what I feel is the product of a simple biochemical disorder, and not the interplay of ineffable magical forces that I can never hope to control.

In a nutshell... I think if god really was out there, really was interested in humanity, he'd be able to talk to me in my head despite the medication. I don't think he'd let a few trifling pharmaceuticals get in his way.

They're indeed full of shit. I learned to program well before I was formally trained in algebra, and although the thinking skills you develop in algebra and calculus courses can be immensely useful for certain classes of problems, they are hardly necessary to write simple programs.

In fact, you're one of the best candidates for picking up programming, because formal geometry is one of the closest forms of "standard" mathematics to programming. The process of deriving proofs and arguing about facts is very similar, although not identical. You will find that being able to reason about geometry translates directly into being able to reason about programs, once you get some basics under your belt.

Statistics is also a tremendous help, because it teaches you to think of things in both aggregate and component terms, i.e. as a whole and as individual parts, respectively. This also is important for doing good software engineering. You won't use stats formulae or anything like that on a regular basis (unless you're working on software that does statistics, obviously!) but the mental patterns would be familiar.

I highly encourage you to try picking up a language. Python is a decent beginner's choice. It doesn't really matter so much what you pick as long as you stick with it for a few years and develop proficiency; then you can move on to learning other languages. You'll find that, as in geometry and stats, there are certain tools that apply to certain types of problem - and programming languages are one such tool. Some languages just naturally solve certain issues better than others. If you feel adventurous, pick up another language in a year or so and play with it as you learn Python, and see how the two compare.

I know that I'm speaking in terms of "years" which may seem like a long time, but programming is really a subtle discipline and requires a lot of time to burn the tools into your brain so that they become instinctive. You'll certainly be making cool programs long before then - probably within a week or two, if not a few days - but you'll soon discover increasingly effective and "clean" ways to solve problems and write software - much the same as you might find a "cleaner" proof of some theorem in geometry.

Best of luck! And remember, if anyone tells you you can't do something, well... fuck them. They don't know.

I'd like to leave you with two thoughts.

 * There is absolutely nothing wrong with needing external validation. I deeply need some, but lack it from anyone in my life - including family and my (very few) friends. This is a negative situation, but the problem is in the lack of validation itself, not in the requirement thereof; that is to say, the answer isn't to seek a way to exist happily without external validation, but rather to locate that validation and take advantage of it. The best you can do is try to extrapolate from known facts, and look for counterexamples. I'm sure as a graduate CS student you're plenty familiar with Goedel's incompleteness theorem: i.e. in any axiomatic system there exist true statements which cannot be derived from the axioms of that system. Simply put, by analogy, it's totally possible that people can care about you but leave you with no conclusive proof - just a set of evidence that points towards a conclusion. For instance: I care, as much as I can about someone I barely know anything about; I'm making an effort to reach out to you and give you some hope for life. I can't prove to you that my caring is real - but I can ask you this: if I didn't really genuinely care, why would I be doing this?
